processing: An appellation rather than one method: the name covers several teas from the mountain, including the green Mengding Ganlu and Shihua and the yellow Mengding Huangya, each processed in its own way.
harvest_season: Typically spring, as with other fine greens; early-spring leaf was already prized in the Tang dynasty.
appearance_dry: The Ganlu grade has fine, tight, downy strands, green with a hint of yellow.
appearance_wet: Whole strands open up, showing a clear bud and leaf.
taste_profile: Clean, high and lasting aroma with a fresh, mellow taste and a sweet return that holds into the second steep.

brewing.notes: These times suit the green Ganlu style. Use a glass or gaiwan, and do not pour boiling water directly on the fine, downy leaf.

vintage_note: Green styles are sold as the current spring harvest and are best drunk within the year. Check which tea you are buying, since the name spans Ganlu, Shihua, Huangya and others, and yellow Huangya is its own product. The label can also be a brand as well as a place.
description:
Mengding Shan Cha is the tea of Mengding Mountain in Mingshan, Ya'an, in Sichuan. It is less a single tea than a family: Ganlu and Shihua on the green side, Huangya on the yellow. People praise the mountain as much as any one of them.

The mountain matters to the leaf. It is damp and misty, with an average temperature of about 14.5°C and 2,000 to 2,200 mm of rain a year, and that cloud softens the direct sun. Each tea from here is then made in its own way; Ganlu, often rated the best, is a fine, curled, downy green.

In the cup, Ganlu is clear yellow-green with a clean aroma and a sweet, fresh taste, and many drinkers find the second steep richer than the first. Use cooler water and short steeps, because the common mistake is scalding the delicate first infusion.

When buying, ask which tea it is and the picking date. Mengding on its own is a broad label, and it has also been a registered trademark, so it does not by itself tell you which tea or which garden you are getting.

For a neat comparison, try Ganlu next to Huangya: same mountain, two different classes of tea.
history:
Legend credits a Western Han farmer, Wu Lizhen, with planting seven tea bushes on the summit; later gazetteers and stele repeat the story, and the Southern Song is said to have granted him a posthumous title. Firmer evidence comes from the Tang: Li Zhao's Guoshi Bu ranks Mengding Shihua first among the empire's teas, and the tea went to court as tribute from the Tang until the end of the Qing, though the exact starting date varies between accounts.

In the modern era a state tea farm was founded on the mountain in 1963 and the Mengding trademark was registered in 1981. By the early Republican years Huangya had become the leading product. In 2017 Mengding Shan Cha was named among China's ten leading regional tea brands, and it also appears on earlier unofficial lists of famous teas.
